The public release comprises a Grade 2, 6 and 10 microdata including all 16 countries. These learner microdata contain both the learner level assessment and contextual questionnaire data. In addition, each microdata contains responses to the principal, teacher and parent questionnaires.

Each of these sections is described in more detail below.

## Grade 2 student assessment

The PASEC 2024 Grade 2 student assessment was designed to measure foundational literacy and numeracy skills acquired during the early years of primary schooling. Assessments were administered individually (one-on-one) and took approximately 30 minutes per subject (language and mathematics). The assessments were conducted individually by trained administrators over four mornings, with a maximum of 16 learners per selected school divided into two sub-groups from the same class.

## Grade 6 student assessment

Unlike the Grade 2 assessment, the Grade 6 assessment was administered as a group-based written test and consisted entirely of multiple-choice questions (MCQs), with response options coded from 1 to 4. To accommodate the large volume of assessment content, PASEC used a rotating booklet design, whereby students were randomly assigned one of four booklets (A, B, C, or D) within each selected class. The assessment lasted up to two hours per subject.

## Student Reading and Mathematics Proficiency Scores

PASEC uses Item Response Theory (IRT) to estimate student proficiency in reading and mathematics from responses to the assessment items together with background information. These estimates are provided as five plausible values for reading (**LECT_PV1 – LECT_PV5**) and five plausible values for mathematics (**MATHS_PV1 – MATHS_PV5**). The microdata also include plausible values for the various content domains included in each assessment. The PASEC 2024 proficiency scores are reported on the same scale as PASEC 2014 and 2019, which was standardised to have an international mean of 500 and a standard deviation of 100, with each participating country contributing equally to the scaling. The use of common assessment items allows results from 2024 to be compared directly with those from 2014 and 2019.

The scales are divided into a series of proficiency levels that represent increasingly complex knowledge and skills. Each level corresponds to a specific score range and is defined by groups of assessment tasks that share common conceptual and statistical characteristics. Because the levels are hierarchical, students performing at a given level are also expected to be able to complete tasks associated with lower levels.

PASEC defines a **minimum proficiency level** representing the knowledge and skills considered necessary for successful progression through the education system. For mathematics, the minimum proficiency level corresponds to Level 2 in both Grade 2 and Grade 6. For language of instruction, the minimum proficiency level corresponds to Level 3.

For reporting on Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator 4.1.1, the PASEC minimum proficiency level aligns with the SDG minimum proficiency level for Grade 2 (SDG 4.1.1a). In Grade 6, however, the SDG 4.1.1b minimum proficiency level is set one level higher than the PASEC minimum proficiency level.

```{=html}
    <td>Students at this level do not sufficiently demonstrate the skills measured by this test in mathematics. These students struggle with the knowledge and skills of Level 1</td>
  </tr>
</table>
</div>
```

*Source: PASEC 2019 QUALITY OF EDUCATION SYSTEMS IN FRENCH-SPEAKING SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA Table 2.2 pp 53.*

## Grade 2 student contextual questionnaire

The questionnaire was administered one-on-one and took about 15 minutes per student. In the dataset, all Grade 2 student questionnaire variables are identified by the prefix **qe2a**. The questionnaire collected information on living arrangements, pre-primary schooling, languages at home and books at home and school.

## Grade 6 student contextual questionnaire

The Grade 6 student contextual questionnaire was group administered with one interviewer per class and took between 45 and 60 minutes to complete. The contextual questionnaire collected information on learners' personal characteristics, family background, educational resources, and well-being at school. In the dataset, all Grade 6 student questionnaire variables are identified by the prefix **qe6a**.

## Grade 10 student contextual questionnaire
The Grade 10 student contextual questionnaire was also group administered and similar to the Grade 6 questionnaire but with more detailed questions on relationships with others. Variables from the Grade 10 student questionnaire can be identified by the prefix **qec** in the data

## Teacher questionnaire

The teacher survey was completed independently by all teachers in primary schools and Language of Instruction and Mathematics teachers in middle schools. The teacher questionnaire collected detailed information on teachers' individual characteristics, academic and professional qualifications, employment status and remuneration, class characteristics, instructional practices, participation in meetings and supervision activities, working conditions, and the infrastructure and resources available in their classrooms.

In the datasets, teacher questionnaire variables are identified by the prefix **qep** in the Grade 2 and 6 datasets and **qec** in the Grade 10 dataset.

## Principal questionnaire

The principal questionnaire was administered to the principals of all sampled schools and collected contextual information about school leadership, management, and school characteristics. In the datasets, all principal questionnaire variables are identified by the prefix **qde** in Grade 2 and 6 and **qpc** in Grade 10. The questionnaire covers principals' individual characteristics, academic and professional qualifications, employment status and remuneration, school characteristics, management practices, relationships with parents and the wider community, pedagogical and administrative aspects of school operation, the school calendar, and the availability of infrastructure and educational resources.

## Parent questionnaire 

The parent questionnaire focuses mainly on the householdʼs living conditions and education-related spending, the learning materials and educational resources available at home, how the childʼs schooling is supported, parentsʼ involvement in school organizations and activities, and their views on national languages as well as their perceptions of the school. Note that the respondent may be a guardian, and parents may also receive assistance—especially those with lower literacy—when answering the questions. This information is captured in the questionnaire for both parents of primary and lower-secondary students. Parent variables use the prefix **qp** in the Grade 2, Grade 6, and Grade 10 datasets.

## Derived variables

PASEC 2024 includes a number of derived indices that summarise information collected through the student, teacher, and principal questionnaires. These indices were constructed using Item Response Theory (IRT), specifically the Rasch model, in a manner similar to the construction of learner achievement scores. These indices provide ready-made measures of learner, classroom, school, and community contexts and can be used directly in analyses examining factors associated with student achievement. At the student level, no derived indices were created for Grade 2 learners.

## Administrative variables

PASEC 2024 includes several identifiers that enable researchers to uniquely identify records across students, teachers, schools, strata, and countries. These identifiers are essential for accounting for the survey design, and conducting multilevel analyses.

```{=html}
<div class="pasec-table-wrap">
<table class="pasec-data-table">
  <tr>
    <td style="background-color: #002060; color: #FFFFFF">Variable</td>
    <td style="background-color: #002060; color: #FFFFFF">Description</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>ID_TOT</td>
    <td>Unique student identifier</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>ID_ECOLE</td>
    <td>School identifier</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>ID_ELEVE</td>
    <td>Student identifier within a school</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>ID_STRATE</td>
    <td>Stratum identifier within a country</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>ID_PAYS</td>
    <td>Country identifier</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>PAYS</td>
    <td>Country name</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>LANGUE</td>
    <td>Language of assessment</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>rwgt0</td>
    <td>Final student weight</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>rwgt1-rwgt50/100/90</td>
    <td>Replicate weights (50 in Grade 2, 100 in Grade 6 and 90 in Grade 10)</td>
  </tr>
</table>
</div>
```

The primary weight used for student-level analyses is the **final student weight (rwgt0).** This weight incorporates all stages of the sampling process and adjustments for nonresponse. Specifically, it combines the initial school selection weight, adjustments for school nonresponse, the class selection weight (where applicable), the student selection weight, and adjustments for student nonparticipation. As a result, **rwgt0** represents the number of students in the population represented by each sampled learner and should be used in most student-level analyses.

Standard error calculations need to take the three-stage stratified sampling design of PASEC 2024 into account. PASEC 2024 provides 50 replicate weights for Grade 2, 100 replicate weights for Grade 6, and 90 for Grade 10 to calculate the correct sampling variance. Learn more about [replicate weights](c02-replicate-weights.html) and how to use them.
